### Session 6.1


#### 12:45 - 1:35 | Open Publishing Unplugged: Unlocking Creativity and Collaboration

**Workshop**

**Karna Younger et al.** | *Loyola Marymount University*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Abstract
A proven equity strategy in education (Hilton, 2019; Colvard et al., 2018), open educational resources (OER) creation and remixing should be a collaboration to ensure OER are supportive of a inclusive, diverse, and equitable learning experience (Sergiadis et al., 2024). This session offers a behind-the-scenes look at collaboratively guiding 11 teams of 39 faculty from four colleges and universities as they created and remixed OER in 11 different fields of study. Through their community building, the presenters modeled transparency, creativity, and collaboration, creating brave spaces for faculty to explore and share their own OER journeys.

Participants will gain insight into the joys and challenges of managing a large-scale collaboration. Challenges included scheduling across four institutions, creating templates and frameworks to guide the process, and ensuring alignment with diversity, equity, inclusion, and anti-racism (DEIA), accessibility, copyright, and instructional design best practices. To support these efforts, the presenters developed an OER faculty handbook, which includes practical guidance on integrating DEIA into OER, making OER accessible, aligning content with learning objectives, and designing interactivity using Pressbooks and H5P. By simultaneously creating their own OER faculty handbook and transparently sharing their wins and fails, the presenters modeled the process, encouraged faculty to innovate boldly, and celebrated their own learning through presentations, goodie bags, and community recognition.

This session will include live demonstrations of interactive, objective-aligned H5P tools and OER texts in Pressbooks from the OER faculty handbook and faculty teams’ work. Participants will explore sections of the OER faculty handbook, such as the OER Tool Look Book, backward design for OER, and strategies for engaging faculty learners. Group discussions will focus on collaboratively problem-solving challenges in building OER communities and brainstorming strategies for success.
:::

### Session 6.2a


#### 12:45 - 1:05 | MicroDesign in Open/Higher Education

**Practice**

**Hilary Schmidt et al.** | *Thompson Rivers University*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Abstract
In this session, we will briefly define and describe microlearning and explore participants’ prior understanding of and engagement with microlearning as designers, teachers, and learners. We will demonstrate an asynchronous, online microlearning project that we created. We will discuss instructional design considerations and support participants in considering where and how they might create their own microlearning lessons.

Microlearning is an established technique for learning and development in many workplaces, with the recognition that busy professionals face constraints on their learning time. A microlearning approach is both convenient and effective; it can enhance learning outcomes and improve retention of information and skills, while reducing cognitive load by delivering information in digestible, focused segments (Taylor & Hung, 2022). Shifting from a more traditional, time-intensive approach, microlearning is tightly focused, aiming to support effective, just-in-time learning (Alias & Razak, 2024). Despite the benefits of microlearning, adoption has been limited in higher education contexts for both faculty and students (Corbeil & Corbeil, 2023; Lockley, 2024).

Harnessing the advantages of a microlearning approach, we created a suite of asynchronous online microlearning lessons (MicroDesign) to enable busy faculty members to grasp fundamentals of open/online course development in interactive, asynchronous online lessons of 5 minutes or less. In the session, we will share an example: a high quality, interactive microlearning lesson that explores copyright compliance (a critical responsibility for course developers, particularly in an open learning context).

In the session, we will tell the “story” of the design process. As well, we will discuss the technology used to build and host MicroDesign, provide additional examples of microlearning for a postsecondary audience, and share a template to guide participants’ planning of their own microlearning possibilities.
:::

### Session 6.2b


#### 1:05 - 1:25 | Virtual Reality Museums: Redefining Engagement and Understanding in Cultural Heritage

**Practice**

**Yuning Gao** | *New York University*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Abstract
This session explores the development of a Virtual Reality (VR) museum dedicated to the banjo, tracing its cultural and historical significance. Designed as part of a graduate research project, this immersive learning environment aims to enhance accessibility, engagement, and storytelling within digital museum experiences. By leveraging design thinking principles, 3D modeling, and interactive elements, the VR museum bridges gaps in traditional curation, offering visitors an enriched, self-guided exploration of the instrument’s evolution and social impact. The presentation will outline key phases of the project—from initial research and prototyping to user testing and iteration—highlighting both challenges and unexpected insights. Rooted in a commitment to inclusivity and experiential learning, this work aligns with the conference theme, Reframing Togetherness, by fostering new ways of connecting with history, technology, and diverse audiences. Attendees will gain practical takeaways for integrating VR into educational and cultural spaces, as well as insights into designing immersive experiences that prioritize accessibility and engagement.
:::

### Session 6.2c


#### 1:25 - 1:45 | AI as Creative Writing Coach: Exploring Human-AI Collaboration in Creative Writing Learning

**Research**

**Cinzia Pusceddu** | *Affiliation*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Abstract
What role can AI play in creative writing learning beyond simply generating or editing text? My research investigates the potential of generative AI as a collaborative partner in creative learning, focusing on its role in prompting the writer’s reflection rather than contributing directly to the writing itself. Drawing on enactivist theory’s (1) view of learning as emerging through interaction and posthumanist perspectives on non-human agency, I intend to examine how sustained AI-human dialogue influences creative development and writing processes. The research combines autoethnography to document the writer’s subjective experience with thing ethnography (2) to capture AI’s role as an active participant, producing both theoretical insights into human-AI collaboration and a literary work that emerges through this process. The resulting creative piece serves as both artwork and case study, embodying the research findings and demonstrating how AI-human creative partnerships affect creative choices, self-reflection, and artistic development.
:::

## 1:45 - 2:00 | Break

## 2:00 - 3:00 | Concurrent Session 7

### Session 7.1


#### 2:00 - 2:50 | Exploring the Intersection of Agriculture, Technology, and Game-Based Learning

**Workshop**

**Patricia Dennis** | *Independent*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Abstract
This conference session, “Exploring the Intersection of Agriculture, Technology, and Game-Based Learning: Empowering Students to Investigate Beneficial Pollinator Bugs with Minecraft Education,” will delve into the innovative integration of agriculture and technology through game-based learning (GBL). Recognizing the critical role of pollinator bugs in agriculture, this session will demonstrate how Minecraft Education can be leveraged as a powerful tool to engage students in understanding and preserving these essential species. Participants will experience a live demo play of the designated Minecraft Education adventure, showcasing how interactive gameplay can simulate real-world agricultural environments. This immersive experience will allow students to investigate the life cycles, habitats, and contributions of pollinator bugs to ecosystems and food production. The session will also cover strategic and beneficial note-taking methods to enhance learning outcomes. Attendees will explore practical strategies for educators to incorporate technology and GBL into their curricula, fostering student engagement and enhancing STEM education. By blending these elements, educators can inspire students to develop a deeper appreciation for environmental sustainability and agricultural science, equipping them with the knowledge and skills needed to address future challenges in food security and biodiversity conservation. Attendees will leave with actionable insights and resources to implement this innovative approach in their own educational settings.
:::

### Session 7.2


#### 2:00 - 2:50 | Educational Pathways to Access, Support, Hope, Transformation, and Opportunities (ePASHTO)

**Practice**

**Hafizullah Abram**, **Paula MacDowell** & **Marguerite Koole** | *University of Saskatchewan*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Abstract
In August 2021, the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan. Their policies resulted in 1.4 million girls losing access to education (Pan, 2023) with both secondary and tertiary education forbidden. While access to primary education is permitted, 30% of young girls never attend for sociocultural, economic, and safety reasons. Female teachers and professors are no longer permitted to work. The humanitarian costs of barring women and girls from basic education is significant on personal, social, and economic levels.

Distance education and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) could offer some pragmatic solutions. “Artificial intelligence refers to the ability of computer systems to mimic human intelligence” (Bowen and Watson, 2024, p. 16). Generative means that “they can produce novel outputs of the same general kind as their training data” (Vallor, 2024, p. 19). GenAI trains on images, text, sound, and even video. The large language models basically predict which words connect to each other. Mollick (2024) describes GenAI as an “elaborate autocomplete” like what is on a smartphone (p. 9). Nevertheless, GenAI can interact with a human-like competence which—albeit has limitations—can still offer a means of supporting learners.

GenAI could provide a way to interact and practice language skills, receive personalized feedback, and access educational content tailored to individual needs. Abram (2025) argues that GenAI tools can assist with translation, adaptive learning, creation of and modification of lessons, motivation, interaction, as well as assessment and evaluation. In this online presentation, we will present and discuss a series of vignettes. Each vignette will provide three educational scenarios faced by women and girls in Afghanistan. We will address biases, hallucinations, social justice, and the possible goals of ‘big tech’. We will examine how GenAI can 1) help learning/teaching, 2) hinder learning/teaching, and/or 3) present risks.

Any solutions to the problem of access to education must address the current socio-cultural, political, economic, geographic, and infrastructural conditions of Afghanistan. Years of war interrupting school attendance and now the prohibition of education for roughly half of the population (women) has resulted in large learning gaps and very diverse learning needs across the entire population (Abrams, 2025). With this in mind, this presentation will not only explore GenAI opportunities but also the risks for Afghan women and girls—including the risk of doing nothing (Abram, 2025).
:::
